stances.claim: Critics misread Disini v. SOJ (Feb 11, 2014) when they claim it held libel and cyberlibel are 'really one and the same crime' -- the decision held only that cyberlibel is not a NEW crime since Article 353/355 already punishes libel and that cyberlibel involves 'similar means'; this was constitutional reasoning, not a holding on identity-of-offense or unity-of-prescription.
stances.rhetorical_move: close-reading rebuttal (correcting a popular misreading of a constitutional case)

stances.claim: Libel and cyberlibel belong to the same genre of defamation crimes but are different and distinct offenses -- the murder/homicide analogy clarifies: both are the killing of a person, but murder is qualified by treachery or premeditation and carries a heavier penalty; cyberlibel is defamation qualified by computer technology, making it more obnoxious because it spreads farther and faster.
stances.rhetorical_move: genus-species analogy (murder/homicide as teaching frame for libel/cyberlibel)

stances.claim: Cyberlibel is constitutional only for the original author of the post -- VOID and UNCONSTITUTIONAL for those who merely receive and react to it -- establishing that liability does not flow to commenters, sharers, or reactors.
stances.rhetorical_move: Disini-doctrine restatement (clean summary of the constitutional architecture)

stances.claim: PH libel/cyberlibel laws do NOT violate the ICCPR because the Penal Code recognizes truth as a defense subject to good-motives-and-justifiable-ends qualification, and the UN Human Rights Committee did not enjoin PH to decriminalize libel -- it only suggested careful crafting so as not to stifle freedom of expression, which 'carries with it special duties and responsibilities.'
stances.rhetorical_move: international-law-compatibility argument (using ICCPR text and UNHRC posture to defend domestic libel regime)

stances.claim: Even assuming Wilfredo Keng has attained 'public figure' status (Forbes Top 40, scholarship and sports donations of ~P2M/year), Judge Montesa found ACTUAL malice in addition to PRESUMED malice -- based on (a) Santos writing without verification, (b) violation of Rappler's own accuracy/truth/fairness/balance standard as testified by defense witness Hofileña, and (c) seven months of refusing to publish Keng's side; only by testifying could Ressa and Santos have rebutted this and secured outright acquittal.
stances.rhetorical_move: even-if-arguendo concession + three-evidence rebuttal-mapping (taking the strongest defense premise and showing why it still fails)

stances.claim: Prescription -- even of a guilty defendant -- simply means that the passage of time bars further penalization; how that applies to Ressa's case will be explained in the next Sunday column.
stances.rhetorical_move: definitional teaser (closing one column with the conceptual setup for the next)

notable_anecdotes: The murder/homicide analogy -- 'Homicide is the killing of a person. Murder is also the killing of a person, but is a separate crime that carries a heavier penalty' -- one of CJ's cleanest pedagogical analogies, deployed to clarify the libel/cyberlibel relationship in two lines.
The 'more obnoxious' framing repeated three times (Q2, Q3) -- turning the heavier-penalty rationale into a moral as well as legal claim.

Wilfredo Keng's specific public-presence indicators -- Forbes 'Top 40 Richest,' 'low-key figure in business with a massive fortune,' scholarship and sports donations of P2M each year -- preserved verbatim from Keng's own testimony to dramatize the public-figure question.

The three pillars of actual-malice evidence (Santos wrote without verification; contrary to Rappler's own standard as testified by Hofileña; seven-month refusal to publish Keng's side) -- making this column the cleanest single-paragraph summary of the trial court's malice finding.

Defense witness Hofileña's testimony being used AGAINST the defense -- establishing Rappler's own accuracy/truth/fairness standard and showing how Santos's article failed it -- the most damaging self-inflicted single piece of evidence in the case.
The seven Q/A format itself -- unusual for CJ, demonstrating his stated practice (echoed in C54) of replying to relevant emailed questions.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban devotes a Q&A column to seven reader follow-up questions on the previous week's Maria Ressa cyberlibel analysis. He corrects the misreading that Disini v. SOJ (February 11, 2014) held libel and cyberlibel are 'really one and the same crime' -- the case said only that cyberlibel is not a NEW crime, since Article 353/355 already punishes libel and the Cybercrime Law merely affirms that online defamation is 'similar means.' Using a murder/homicide analogy -- both are the killing of a person, but murder is qualified by treachery and carries a heavier penalty -- he explains that libel and cyberlibel belong to the same genre but are distinct offenses, with cyberlibel made 'more obnoxious' by computer technology that spreads defamation farther and faster. He restates Disini's architecture: cyberlibel is VALID and CONSTITUTIONAL for the original author but VOID and UNCONSTITUTIONAL for those who merely receive and react. PH libel laws do not violate the ICCPR because the Penal Code recognizes truth (subject to good-motives qualification) as a defense, and the UN Human Rights Committee did not enjoin decriminalization. Even assuming Wilfredo Keng has attained public-figure status (Forbes 'Top 40 Richest,' scholarship and sports donations of P2M/year), Judge Montesa found ACTUAL malice in addition to PRESUMED malice based on three evidence pillars from the trial record: Santos wrote the article sans verification; this contradicted Rappler's own accuracy/truth/fairness standard as testified by defense witness Chay Hofileña; and Rappler refused for seven months to publish Keng's side despite numerous follow-ups. Only testifying could have rebutted this and secured outright acquittal -- but the accused did not, and were convicted. He closes by defining prescription ('the accused, even if guilty, can no longer be penalized due to the passing of time') and promising the next Sunday's column will explain how it would apply on appeal.
